name: Carla Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing chemistry, so most weeks I'm in a lab three afternoons and in lectures the rest. I rent a room in a shared house with three others near the train station, and I tutor teenagers in maths and science in the evenings, about eight hours a week at fifteen pounds an hour. My mum is a single parent who works in a dental surgery and can't help much with money. I use AI every day, to explain things I missed, to plan my week and to check my lab reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a relief, and a bit of a letdown, since I find it all exciting. I'd tell my housemates that it's still a useful tool, just not a revolution. I'd probably say to my tutoring students that the basics matter as much as ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us it means more of the same: finish my degree, find a job in a lab or industry. I'm pragmatic, so I'd just carry on. The real pressure is rent and the loan. I've got a few weeks of cushion at best, and my tutoring is what keeps me afloat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the tutoring and try to add two more students. I'd use my AI tools to cut my prep time, which gives me more hours for paid work. I'd apply for the summer lab placement the department advertises, since it pays a bit. I wouldn't change the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A little flat, honestly, because I like a bit of change. But it's a steady sort of feeling, and I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does tutoring fit in with the AI tools you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I make practice questions with it, then check every answer myself because it gets some chemistry wrong. My students don't know that, so I'm careful. If a parent found out I used it, I'd say yes, I check it, and the questions are better than what I could write in the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if your tutoring dries up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to a supermarket or a bar for cash. I did bar work last summer, so I know how it goes. Rent is four hundred and ten a month, so I'd need about twelve hours a week to cover it.

say: It's a useful tool, just not a **revolution**.
I'd tell my tutoring students that the basics matter as much as ever.
think: It means more of the same: finish the degree and find a lab or industry job. The real pressure is **rent**.
My tutoring is what keeps me afloat.
do: Keep **tutoring** and add two more students.
Use AI tools to cut my prep time, freeing hours for paid work.
Apply for the summer lab placement.
feel: Fine and a little flat, but **steady** enough to plan.
S0.quote: Rent is four hundred and ten a month, so I'd need about twelve hours a week to cover it.
fieldNote: Carla already uses AI daily and treats a plateau as a chance to earn more by saving **prep** time.
She is honest about checking its chemistry because it gets some answers wrong.

steps.text: Take on two more tutoring students at fifteen pounds an hour
Use AI to draft practice questions, then check every answer
Apply for the department's paid summer lab placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about time, and I'd mean it. I'd tell the department that we need practical lessons on AI in lab work, not just a warning. To my housemates I'd say learn the tools or someone who does will get your job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be excited and a bit nervous. Chemistry has a lot of data crunching and report writing that AI could do for me, and also for companies instead of hiring juniors. But someone needs to run the instruments and judge whether results make sense. I want to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to run the instruments really well, and take a data science option. I'd build a portfolio of lab projects that use AI to analyse results. I'd keep tutoring, and I'd pitch a small service helping school students use AI for study properly, which could earn me more per hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, with a knot in my stomach. It's like standing on a surfboard: I'm not falling yet, but I know it might happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the small service look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A one-hour session on how to use the tools to study without cheating, for parents and students, at twenty pounds a head. I'd run it in the library or online. Schools are confused about it, and I think there's a gap I could fill while I'm a student.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone's doing it. If all the chemists can use the tools, then the edge disappears. So I'd need the lab skills as well, the real hands-on stuff, because a machine can't pipette for me, at least not for a while.

say: Learn the **tools**, or someone who does will get your job.
The department needs practical lessons on AI in lab work, not just a warning.
think: Data crunching and report writing go to AI, but someone has to **judge** whether results make sense.
I want to be that person.
do: Learn to run the **instruments** really well and take a data science option.
Build a portfolio of lab projects that use AI to analyse results.
Pitch a small paid session on using AI to study properly.
feel: **Energised**, with a knot in my stomach, like standing on a surfboard.
S1.quote: A machine can't pipette for me, at least not for a while.
fieldNote: Carla sees the shift as an **opening**: someone has to judge the machine's results, and she wants to be that person.
Her side-service idea comes from a gap she noticed at schools she tutors for.

steps.text: Build a portfolio of lab projects that use AI for analysis
Take a data science option alongside the chemistry degree
Run a paid study-skills session on using AI properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest thing that's ever happened and we're not ready. I'd say it loudly, to friends, and I'd go to any meeting the uni runs about it. But I'd also tell them to use the tools and prepare, because saying it's bad doesn't help you pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared and I'd also feel a weird thrill. Two years means I'm still in my degree when thinking work goes. I might finish in a different economy. Mum's dental surgery would last longer than most, but I have no savings, and there'd be no one to bail me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go very practical. I'd take every paid hour I could, including more tutoring, and keep my costs down. I'd look for the lab technician route, which is hands-on, and ask the department about earning while I finish. I'd also use the tools to build something I could sell, even a small thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and wired. I'd sleep badly but I'd be making lists in the dark. It's the way I cope, and it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd build to sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a revision pack for chemistry students, made with AI and checked by me. At five pounds a pack, I'd need two hundred sales to make something. It's a long shot, but it's a way to learn how to sell something before the job market gets difficult.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is two years different from the longer ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time for the master's or a slow route. It's about what I can do now with the skills I have, and keeping cash. Longer timelines let me invest in learning, and this one just says survive.

say: This is the **biggest** thing that's ever happened and we're not ready.
Use the tools and prepare, because saying it's bad doesn't pay rent.
think: I'd be scared with a weird **thrill**, since I'd still be in my degree when thinking work goes.
I have no savings and no one to bail me out.
do: Take every paid **hour** I can, including more tutoring, and keep costs down.
Look for the hands-on lab technician route.
Build a small revision pack to sell.
feel: Anxious and **wired**, making lists in the dark.
S2.quote: Longer timelines let me invest in learning, and this one just says survive.
fieldNote: Carla's reaction is practical: **cash** first, then a small product she can sell to learn how.
She names the difference two years makes, no time to invest in learning, only survival.

steps.text: Make a chemistry revision pack with AI and sell it at five pounds
Cut costs and save every spare pound from tutoring
Ask the department about lab technician jobs while I study
Use AI tools to cut my prep time and add students

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent amount of time and we shouldn't waste it. I'd tell friends to use the tools in their degree now. I'd also push the uni to run proper career sessions, because lecturers don't know either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I'd feel hopeful. I'd graduate in 2029, so I'd have a couple of years of working with AI before robots reach the lab. If I've built the skills, I could be useful. It's not a guarantee, and I'd be nervous about the first job, but I'd feel like I'm in the game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep tutoring, build a portfolio and aim for a placement year in industry. I'd save a cushion of about a thousand pounds, which I'd get to over two years. I'd also apply for a master's, probably in analytical chemistry, which is part lab and part data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic and a bit tense. I like deadlines, so a five-year one is good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a placement year look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for a company doing quality testing or research for a year, paid. It's usually about twenty thousand, which would clear the rent and give me contacts. I'd ask the careers office this month about which firms take first-years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the master's idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Debt. A master's could put another ten thousand on my loan. I'd only do it if a firm paid part, or if I'd got a good placement first. I'm happy to wait to decide.

say: Five years is a **decent** amount of time and we shouldn't waste it.
The uni should run proper career sessions, because lecturers don't know either.
think: I'd feel **hopeful**, with a couple of years working with AI before robots reach the lab.
I'd be nervous about the first job, but in the game.
do: Keep tutoring, build a **portfolio** and aim for a paid placement year in industry.
Save a cushion of about a thousand pounds over two years.
Consider a master's in analytical chemistry.
feel: **Optimistic** and a bit tense, because I like deadlines.
S3.quote: A master's could put another ten thousand on my loan.
fieldNote: Carla ties more time to a concrete route: a paid **placement** year, a cushion, and a master's only if funded.
She keeps debt in mind and is happy to delay the big decision.

steps.text: Ask the careers office about paid placement-year firms
Save a thousand pounds over two years
Keep tutoring and add a couple more students

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. I'd say it with a bit of guilt, because not everyone has the same room to move. I'd tell my friends to keep their options open and try small things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel pretty calm. I'd have a degree, maybe a master's, several years in a job and the money to cope. I'd also have the habit of learning new tools, which is the real skill. My worry would be that the world changes in a different way than expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take a placement year, and work for a few years in a lab or on the data side. I'd keep experimenting with new tools, and I'd save toward a deposit on a flat. I'd also help my mum, who'd be nearing retirement by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. I'd probably get on with life and think about the big thing now and then, as a background hum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your mum in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help her think about what she'd do if the dental practice used more automation, maybe move into admin or training. She's good with people. I'd also help her get a bit of savings, so she isn't depending on one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in the second half of the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably leading a small team that runs the AI tools on lab data, and doing a part-time master's. I'd be about twenty-six, still renting, still tutoring a little because I like it. It might be a bit like now, with better kit.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, though not everyone has the same room to move.
Keep your options open and try small things.
think: I'd feel pretty **calm**, with a degree, experience, savings and the habit of learning new tools.
The worry is the world changing in an unexpected way.
do: Finish the degree, take a **placement** year and work in a lab or on the data side.
Save toward a flat deposit and keep experimenting with new tools.
Help my mum prepare for the dental practice automating.

S4.quote: I'd also have the habit of learning new tools, which is the real skill.
fieldNote: Carla thinks the real **skill** is the habit of learning new tools, and counts herself lucky to have the room to try.
She plans around her mum's job as much as her own.

steps.text: Take a placement year then work in a lab on the data side
Help my mum plan for the dental practice automating

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years. That's the one where I have the least time and no cushion, and I'd be doing my best on very little. What would help is good information early, paid placements, and the uni opening the labs and tools to students for free.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that being adaptable isn't the same as being safe. I use these tools every day and I still have no cushion. Knowing how to swim doesn't help if the pool's empty.

headlineQuote: Being adaptable isn't the same as being safe. I use these tools every day and I still have no cushion.
portrait: Carla is a 19-year-old **chemistry** student in a shared house, tutoring teens to pay rent while her single mum can't help.
She is centre and adaptive: she uses AI daily, checks its chemistry and values learning new tools.
Her plans are practical and moneyed: more tutoring, a revision pack, a paid placement year.
She says being adaptable isn't the same as being safe when you have no cushion.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most because she'd have the least time and no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Good early information, **paid** placements, and free access to the labs and tools for students.
